terms.comment: A plot sworn to by several, mostly against the state or its rulers; conjūrātiōnem facere, to form a plot. First a swearing together, and so any league: Laches in Terence complains of the conjūrātiō of all women (Ter. Hec. 198, Lewis & Short, at Hec. 2.1.1). The plotters are conjūrātī.

evidence: Cic. Sull. 70: contrā rem pūblicam (Lewis & Short)
Caes. BG 2.3: contrā populum Rōmānum (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: To swear together; in a bad sense, very often, to conspire, with contrā, in or ut.

terms.gloss: a plot, a trap laid for someone
evidence: Cic. Rosc. Am. 26: īnsidiās parāre (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Q. Fr. 2.3.4: vītae alicujus īnsidiās facere (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: First an ambush; then any plot or trap laid for one person, by one or by many: īnsidiās facere, parāre, struere alicui, to plot against someone.

terms.gloss: to work at, to scheme, to plot
evidence: Cic. Rep. 2.60: dē occupandō rēgnō mōliēns (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: To set something heavy in motion, and so to work hard at, to contrive; with īnsidiās, fugam, nova (revolution), to plot it. Not a word for plotting by itself.

phrases.latin: Is … rēgnī cupiditāte inductus conjūrātiōnem nōbilitātis fēcit
phrases.english: He, led on by desire for the throne, formed a plot among the nobles

phrases.latin: nam sī omnia facienda sint, quae amīcī velint, nōn amīcitiae tālēs, sed conjūrātiōnēs putandae sint
phrases.english: for if we must do everything our friends want, such ties should be called conspiracies, not friendships

sources: Lewis & Short: conjuratio · Lewis & Short: conjuro · Lewis & Short: insidiae · Lewis & Short: molior
